We sincerely thank the reviewer iQd3 for their valuable and constructive suggestions. Thank you for acknowledging that the video-based data collected from smartphones enables the capture of dynamic retinal characteristics, such as vessel pulsations. We address the reviewer's concerns as follows.

**Q1: Have metrics such as inter-rater reliability been incorporated to assess the consistency of annotations made by different clinicians?**

**R1:** To ensure the consistency and reliability of annotations provided by different clinicians, we employ an inter-rater reliability assessment on spatial segmentation annotations. After every 100 annotations, we randomly select 5 images from each clinician and reassign them to another clinician for independent annotation. The Intersection over Union (IoU) scores are then calculated between the pairs of annotations, and they are used to measure the consistency of the annotations. If an IoU score is lower than 0.95, a quality check will be manually performed by a third clinician. Otherwise, we will consider the annotations made by clinicians to be of good quality. As for the temporal annotations, each video has been annotated by three clinicians and the presence/absence and duration labels of SVPs are confirmed by the majority voting.

**Q2: The involvement of a model for certain annotations, trained on a subset of labeled data, raises the need to elucidate the model's accuracy and how the remaining dataset's predictions were validated by human raters.**

**R2:** Thank you for the comment. In fact, the spatial and temporal annotations of all the videos are manually labeled. Therefore, our original annotation process does not involve any model training. We thank the reviewer's suggestion. In the future, when we annotate more video frames, we will adopt the suggested method.

**Q3: Lack of demographic information.**

**R3:** Thank you for your insightful suggestion. We further provide the gender information for each video in our dataset and hope this piece of information can shed some light on the relationship between genders and retinal conditions. The file is provided [**here**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1f0Z3SWnbRIQZqRi_banIKO3_TabDEfvh/view?usp=drive_link).

**Q4: Would it be possible to share the data distribution between normal and diseased eyes, and the variety of eye diseases represented in the dataset?**

**R4:** The distribution of normal and diseased eyes will be included in our dataset. It can be found [**here**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1B5Ln4K9zRKjabmdnx7KNBW6t7zBFRXMb/view?usp=drive_link). Since the data are collected from the patients who visited the clinics for glaucoma examination, the available eye disease label is glaucoma. Moreover, SVPs reflect the anomaly of inter-cranial pressure, and we also provide the disease names in the [**Link**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Uj4udJCJG1PGlbpS73XD4nrg2nPxLQwo/view?usp=drive_link). 

**Q5: Evaluating the model's performance across different clinics and between normal and diseased cases to further understand potential domain gaps.**

**R5:** Thank you for the constructive suggestion. (1) We focus on binary segmentation and SVP detection. We then test our best-performing model (Mask2Former with the Swin Transformer backbone and I3D model) on each clinic test data. Here, we denote the four clinics as P, Q, R, and S. The vessel segmentation performance across different clinics is reported as follows:

**Table 1. Binary segmentation results of Mask2Former across different clinics.**

|---------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| mIoU    | 73.85 | 72.00 | 70.89 | 75.33 |
| mAcc    | 79.63 | 77.72 | 75.63 | 81.78 |
| mFscore | 81.35 | 80.54 | 78.38 | 82.27 |

**Table 2. Evaluation of the I3D model on SVP detection across different clinics.**
| Clinics |  P    |  Q    |  R    |  S    | 
|---------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| Acc     | 64.58 | 50.00 | 60.00 | 58.33 |
| AUROC   | 70.28 | 66.67 | 58.83 | 54.32 |
| Recall  | 65.38 | 66.67 | 90.00 | 51.85 |

As shown in Table 1 and Table 2, for both vessel segmentation and SVP detection, the performance of the model on different clinics is different, indicating that domain gaps exist in different clinics. 

(2) Similarly, we also report the binary segmentation performance on normal and diseased retinal videos below:

**Table 3. Binary segmentation results of Mask2Former on diseased/normal videos.**
|Eye Condition|	Diseased |Normal|
|-------------|--------|------|
| mIoU 	      |74.25   |73.96 |

As shown in Table 3, the segmentation results of the baseline model for both diseased and normal eye videos are close, indicating the domain discrepancy between the diseased and normal videos is marginal in the context of retinal vessel segmentation. **Q5: Claim on the most challenging dataset.**

**R5:** The existing datasets are acquired using benchtop devices and offer high-quality images of retinal vessels. In contrast, our dataset consists of videos captured with handheld devices, which are susceptible to various factors. These factors include motion blur and significant changes in illumination due to eye movements or the unsteady hands of clinicians, as well as blocked views resulting from eye blinks. Hence, in the "Conclusion" section, we stated that our dataset is **more challenging** compared to the existing datasets. 

**Q6: The statistics of diseased and healthy eyes.**

**R7:** Thank you for the suggestion. For each video, we currently annotate two frames for the spatial segmentation masks. The second frame is selected in order to capture most of the areas of vessel areas in an eye. Thus, it can provide complementary vessel areas to those in the first frame. As shown in Table 1, when tested on the third dataset CHASEDB, models trained on RVD achieve lower performance compared to those trained on DRIVE. This indicates our dataset exhibits a larger domain gap from the existing datasets. We added these results in the revision (Section C.3.4).

**Q2: Given that annotations and frame selection procedures are manual and reliant on the annotator's expertise, how much do these aspects depend on the individual annotator? Could multiple annotators be engaged for less biased annotations?**

**R2:** Thank you for the comments. In the process of frame selection, clinicians initially choose the first frame and then proceed to manually assess the quality of the automatically chosen second frame. The criteria for frame selection are rooted in factors such as image quality, visibility of vessels, and the absence of obstructions, making them objective in nature. Clinicians are unlikely to exhibit bias towards specific frames.

For spatial vessel annotations, clinicians employ ImageJ software for vessel delineation and detail scrutiny. Here, we incorporate inter-rater reliability using the IoU metric to ensure the consistency of annotations across different annotators. Specifically, after every 100 annotations, we randomly select 5 frames from each clinician and then reassign these frames to another clinician for annotations. If the IoU is lower than 0.95, the annotations are manually reviewed by a third clinician. For the temporal SVP annotations, each video has been annotated by three clinicians to reduce annotation bias. We have clarified these details in the main paper (Line 199-205).

**Q3: Clarification on the annotation status about the presence or absence of SVP?**

We sincerely thank the reviewer LKzk for the very valuable comments. We are encouraged that the reviewer acknowledges that the clinical problem is well-motivated and the dataset is relatively large. Here, we would like to respond to the issues and hope that our responses will address the concerns.

**Q1: What is the global prevalence of the handheld protocol with the fundus camera lens?**

**R1:** Smartphone-based fundus imaging devices are mainly divided into two groups: (1) direct ophthalmoscopy and (2) indirect ophthalmoscopy. Direct ophthalmoscopy only provides a ***narrow*** field of view of the retina similar to traditional ophthalmoscopes. Indirect ophthalmoscopy uses binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy (BIO) lenses that produce a ***wider*** field of view. Nowadays, almost all eye examinations by ophthalmologists utilize the indirect ophthalmoscope [A]. The majority of devices incorporate a 20 or 28 dioptre lens system. The devices we used in the paper are also based on indirect ophthalmoscopy.

[A] Prakalapakorn, S. G., et al. Evaluation of an indirect ophthalmoscopy digital photographic system as a retinopathy of prematurity screening tool. Journal of American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus, 2014.

**Q2: Is there any bias in how/where these images are collected based on the availability of handheld devices (or a lack of availability of benchtop devices)?**

**R2:** Thank you for the comment. We have tried our best to reduce foreseeable biases in three aspects. First, videos are collected across four different clinics. Doing so significantly eliminates the data collection bias caused by a certain clinician as well as increases the diversity of data collection environments. Second, we use two types of devices (with iphone 8 and ipad mini 4 imagining sensors) to further reduce the imaging bias caused by devices. Lastly, we collect videos from a large number of patients, thus increasing the diversity of collected samples.

**Q3: Domain gaps within the dataset.**

**R3:** In our dataset, videos are acquired by using two types of camera models. As suggested, we have incorporated the imaging device label into each video in our dataset [**link**](https://drive.google.com/file/d/11BgZACOE-cQsa_Saydlh0q9tW7rIE1Ks/view?usp=drive_link).

To study the domain gaps between the data collected from different devices, we focus on the binary segmentation task and adopt the best-performing model mask2former with the Swin transformer backbone. Specifically, we train the model on data collected from one device and test on that of another device. The results are shown in the following Table:

**Table 1. Results of models trained on one device and tested on another device.**


|  DEIVCE |Metric| **DEVICE 1** | **DEVICE 2** |
|------------|-------|-----------|------|
|            | mIoU | 69.37         | 71.07  |

|             | mIoU | 68.53       | 70.98 |  
| **DEVICE 2**| mAcc | 74.2       | 77.99  | 
|             | mFscore | 77.85    | 80.04 |


The performance of the models varies slightly across different devices. This suggests that the variations in the data collection process introduce some domain gaps. We added the results in the supplementary (Section C.3.2).

**Q4: The limitations of this work.**

**R4:** Due to the page limit, we discussed the potential limitation in “Broader Impacts Statement” in the supplementary material. Although our RVD is the largest dataset for retinal vessel segmentation to date (635 videos with annotations), its scale can be further improved in the future. Compared to benchtop devices, the videos captured by handheld devices might be affected by more factors, such as shaking hands of operators, and unconscious eye movements or blinks during recording. Thus, recorded videos would inevitably contain some noise. Hence, the captured data will require more sophisticated data cleaning and preprocessing strategies to eliminate the impacts of low-quality frames and ensure the reliability of the data.

We sincerely thank the reviewer 1P9Y for the constructive comments and suggestions. We are glad that the reviewer acknowledges that our work provides the first video-based retinal vessel dataset, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of retinal functionality and vasculature structure.

**Q1: Result evaluation using DICE scores.**

**R1:** In our paper, we employ mFscore (*i.e.*, macro-averaged F1-score, which treats all classes equally) for both binary and multi-class image segmentation tasks. Since the F1 score is also known as the DICE score in binary classification or segmentation tasks [A], the mFscore essentially equals to the DICE scores for segmentation tasks. We have clarified this in the revision (Line 291-293). 

[A] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-score

**Q2: Apart from DeepLabV3 and Mask2Former, providing the results of other SOTA segmentation methods?**

**R2:** Due to the page limit, we indeed provided the results of other state-of-the-art architectures, *e.g.*, PSP-NET, Segmenter, and FCN. Please check Table 2 in the supplementary material. 

**Q3: Analysis of computational efficiency.**

**R3:** Thank you for the suggestion. We analyze the computational operations (*i.e.*, GFLOPs) and inference time for the trained models. Specifically, for models trained with spatial annotations, we analyze Mask2Former (M2F) and DeepLabv3 (DLV3) with different backbones. The results are presented as follows:

**Table 1. Computational efficiency of Mask2Former (M2F) and DeepLabv3 (DLV3) with different backbones (Resolution: 512x512 pixels).**

| Model                |                           |     |     | M2F     |     |     |     | \| | DLV3     ||
|----------------------|-------------------------------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|--|-----|----------|--
| Backbone             | ResNet50                      | ResNet101 | Swin-T | Swin-S | Swin-B-1k | Swin-B-22k | Swin-L | \| | ResNet50 | ResNet101 |
| GFLOPs (G)           | 40                           | 59  | 28  | 36  | 86  | 86  | 160  | \| | 270     | 347     |
| Inference time (ms)  | 27.30                         | 29.7 | 31.3 | 45.3 | 67.2 | 62.8 | 92.2 |  \| | 24.5     | 33.7     |

As indicated in Table 1, models with larger backbones require more computational cost and more inference time. For example, models with Swin-T to Swin-L backbones require more in both GFLOPs and inference time.  However, we notice that the inference time may not linearly grow with GFLOPs, since the inference time can be affected by many factors, *e.g.*, CUDA optimization for different network structures.

For models trained with temporal annotations, we consider SVP detection with different backbones. We provide their GFLOPs and inference time below:

**Table 2. Computational efficiency of models trained with temporal annotations (Resolution: 320x320 pixels).**
| Model | LRCN  |  I3D     |   X3D     |  TSN   |   VTN   |
|-----------|-------|----------|-----------|--------|---------|
| GFLOPs     | 16 | 263     | 180      | 252   | 1374
| Inference time (ms)| 89.0 |  226.7 | 182.8  | 322.3 | 486.2 | 

As shown in Table 2, the speed of models for SVP detection is often within 1 second, *e.g.*, LRCN processes each video in 89 ms on average. The inference time for segmentation and SVP detection is acceptable in practice. We added these discussions in the main paper (Section 4.3).

**Q4: The authors did not mention any negative societal impact or limitations.**

**R4:** We have discussed the social impact and limitations in the ''Broader Impacts Statement". According to the submission guideline, we included this part in the supplementary material.

Societal impact: Handheld fundus imaging devices make the earlier detection and prevention of ocular diseases more accessible and less reliant on expensive, specialized ophthalmic equipment. Thus, providing a handheld fundus video dataset will significantly advance the accessibility of ocular disease diagnosis, thus leading to positive societal impacts, especially in the healthcare sector. Currently, we have not perceived any negative societal impacts of our proposed dataset.

Limitations: Compared to benchtop devices, the videos captured by handheld devices might be affected by more factors, such as unsteady hands of operators, and unconscious eye movements or blinks during recording. Thus, recorded videos would inevitably contain some noise. Hence, the captured data will require more sophisticated data cleaning and preprocessing strategies to eliminate the impacts of low-quality frames and ensure the reliability of the data.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper highlights the significance of retinal vasculature patterns in tracking morphological changes related to ocular diseases. Existing methods rely on image-based datasets, limiting their ability to capture dynamic characteristics like vessel pulsations. To address this, the paper introduces the first video-based retinal vessel dataset (RVD) recorded using smartphones, providing spatial and temporal annotations.

strengths.value:
The dataset utilizes videos captured from smartphone-based devices, allowing for continuous observation of retinal vessels and capturing dynamic changes over time. This provides a more comprehensive understanding of retinal functionality and vasculature structure compared to static image-based datasets.

The dataset offers three distinct levels of spatial annotations, including binary vessel masks, general vein-artery masks, and fine-grained vein-artery masks. These detailed annotations enable researchers to analyze the vessel structure at various granularities, catering to specific clinical purposes and facilitating accurate vessel segmentation.

This dataset also provides temporal annotations of spontaneous retinal venous pulsations (SVP), which reveal the complex dynamics of retinal vasculature. These temporal annotations are essential for assessing pulsatile variations in retinal vessels and diagnosing temporally-dependent ocular diseases, enhancing the dataset's potential for ocular disease diagnosis.

summary_and_contributions.value:
The submission introduces the first video-based retinal vessel dataset (RVD) collected using smartphone-based devices. The dataset contains 635 videos with detailed vessel annotations, capturing continuous changes in retinal vessels. Unlike traditional image-based datasets, RVD allows the analysis of dynamic retinal characteristics, such as vessel pulsations, which are essential for a comprehensive understanding of retinal functionality and vasculature structure.

The dataset provides spatial and temporal annotations. In the spatial dimension, three levels of annotations are offered: binary vessel masks, general vein-artery masks, and fine-grained vein-artery masks, tailored to specific clinical purposes. In the temporal dimension, annotations of retinal vessel fluctuations in the optic disk region are provided, including maximal and minimal pulse widths and the existence of spontaneous retinal venous pulsations (SVP), aiding in the detection of ocular diseases.

strengths.value:
1. Novel Dataset Format: The RVD introduces a video-based retinal vessel dataset collected from smartphones, which is a departure from traditional image-based datasets. This unique format enables the capture of dynamic retinal characteristics, such as vessel pulsations and temporal variations.

2. Rich Spatial Annotations: The dataset provides three levels of spatial annotations, including binary vessel masks, general vein-artery masks, and fine-grained vein-artery masks. This granularity allows researchers to explore retinal vessel structures at different levels of detail, enhancing the understanding of vessel morphology.

3. Temporal Annotations: The RVD includes temporal annotations, particularly spontaneous retinal venous pulsations (SVP). This sets it apart from other retinal datasets and enables the assessment of vascular pulsations, providing valuable insights for clinical applications.

4. Realistic Factors and Domain Gaps: Unlike image-based datasets captured using expensive ophthalmic equipment, the RVD accounts for realistic factors such as clinician operations, illumination conditions, and patient eye movements. This introduces domain gaps, making the dataset more challenging and fostering innovation in vessel segmentation methods.

5. Benchmarking Opportunities: The RVD facilitates benchmarking state-of-the-art retinal vessel segmentation methods. Researchers can assess the performance of existing techniques on mobile-device-based retinal data, encouraging the development of more robust and effective algorithms.

6. Empowering Mobile Healthcare: By utilizing portable devices for data acquisition, the RVD contributes to the advancement of mobile healthcare solutions. It enables easier and more accessible retinal observation and analysis, potentially benefiting patients in remote or underserved areas with limited access to specialized medical equipment.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Annotation Subjectivity/Quality: The spatial and temporal annotations provided by different clinicians may exhibit variations due to subjective interpretations of vessel boundaries or pulsation patterns. These subjective aspects have the potential to influence the reliability and reproducibility of the annotations. To better assess the consistency of annotations, incorporating metrics like inter-rater reliability would be valuable. Additionally, the involvement of a model for certain annotations, trained on a subset of labeled data, raises the need to elucidate the model's accuracy and how the remaining dataset's predictions were validated by human raters. Sharing the performance of these models and clarifying whether raters inspected and corrected all annotations or only a subset would enhance transparency.

2. Lack of Demographic Information: While the authors state that all patients in the dataset fall within the 50-75 age range, no information about the demographic distribution is provided. Further insights into the distribution of normal versus diseased eyes, along with details about the types of eye diseases represented, would be valuable to readers. Such demographic information could shed light on potential variations in retinal conditions across different populations.

3. Broadening Generalization Studies: In addition to evaluating domain generalization between hand-held and bench-top devices, exploring how the model performs across different institutions (clinics) and disease categories (normal vs. diseased) would be highly intriguing. If available, annotations denoting specific eye diseases or clinic identifiers (using anonymized names like a, b, c, d, etc.) could facilitate the training and testing of domain generalization algorithms that can effectively handle variations across clinics and diseases. Presenting these annotations in a tabular form within the paper would offer readers a comprehensive summary and aid further research in this direction.

ethics.value: The dataset includes videos from patients, raising ethical concerns. However, the authors obtained relevant consent from participants, ensuring anonymity. They followed ethical guidelines, protecting patient privacy through data anonymization. These practices uphold dignity, rights, and dataset reliability.

summary_and_contributions.value: Authors release a retinal video database composed of 635 retinal videos from 450 patients. The dataset comprises ~13K frames and so far is the largest public dataset in the area. The annotations span only 650 samples for 3 different vein related labels. The authors also labeled the dataset for "Retinal Venous Pulsation (SVP)" and peak&trough states of the vessel.

strengths.value:
The dataset is very large and provides different annotations, which are not available as a whole in any other dataset.
Authors provide step by step procedure for the labeling process
The authors also provide baseline AI segmentation and classification models for their dataset and also try to measure the domain gap between their dataset and the other public ones in the literature through these AI models.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
The domain gap claims should be supported with better data and experiments. The experiments presented in Table 4 are useful but not truly indicative of the domain gap. 

Annotations and some of the frame selection procedures are manual, so they are dependent on the annotator's expertise. Authors could have gotten multiple annotators engaged to potentially get less biased annotations that depend on one single annotator's opinion. Overall please elaborate on how much the annotations and frame selection depend on the annotator's expertise. 

 In section 3.3.2 Authors' statement starting as: "Considering the needs of the speciality..." Is the described procedure pending, already done. The language suggests it is pending. Please clarify.

Among all the datasets, FIVES dataset is the closest one to RVD in terms of dataset size. However, the authors did not present any comparative results against this dataset in Table 4. 

In the Conclusions section: The authors state that their dataset is the most challenging dataset. It is not clear how the authors reached to this conclusion.

limitations.value:
The data is collected at multiple centers, so it covers a wide spectrum. 

Even if the authors state that the data also covers both diseased and healthy eyes, the statistics are not presented.

The authors state that they select the sharpest and the most representative frame for the purpose of spatial annotations. Following this statement, in section 3.3.1 authors describe the selection of keyframes for spatial segmentation but sharpness is not a criterion here. Moreover, the role of Keyframe #2 in spatial segmentation is unclear. Overall, authors need to more clearly (and consistently) explain (i) how many frames/video are annotated for spatial structures and (ii) how are these frame(s) selected.

The domain gap claims are weak. The authors try to justify the domain gap between the RVD and other datasets through AI experiments presented in Table 4. The RVD dataset is a lot larger than the other datasets that are used in Table 4. Therefore, it is not clear if the performance differences are a result of the change in training dataset size or domain gap. A good experiment can be training two models with similar amounts of data from 2 different datasets (e.g., one model with RVD and another with DRIVE) and testing these models on a third dataset to measure the domain gap. Please also state with performance metric is used for Table 4 results.

title.value: RVD: A Handheld Device-Based Fundus Video Dataset for Retinal Vessel Segmentation

abstract.value:
Retinal vessel segmentation is generally grounded in image-based datasets collected with bench-top devices. 
The static images naturally lose the dynamic characteristics of retina fluctuation, resulting in diminished dataset richness, and the usage of bench-top devices further restricts dataset scalability due to its limited accessibility. Considering these limitations, we introduce the first video-based retinal dataset by employing handheld devices for data acquisition. The dataset comprises 635 smartphone-based fundus videos collected from four different clinics, involving 415 patients from 50 to 75 years old. It delivers comprehensive and precise annotations of retinal structures in both spatial and temporal dimensions, aiming to advance the landscape of vasculature segmentation. Specifically, the dataset provides three levels of spatial annotations: binary vessel masks for overall retinal structure delineation, general vein-artery masks for distinguishing the vein and artery, and fine-grained vein-artery masks for further characterizing the granularities of each artery and vein. In addition, the dataset offers temporal annotations that capture the vessel pulsation characteristics, assisting in detecting ocular diseases that require fine-grained recognition of hemodynamic fluctuation. In application, our dataset exhibits a significant domain shift with respect to data captured by bench-top devices, thus posing great challenges to existing methods. Thanks to rich annotations and data scales, our dataset potentially paves the path for more advanced retinal analysis and accurate disease diagnosis. In the experiments, we provide evaluation metrics and benchmark results on our dataset, reflecting both the potential and challenges it offers for vessel segmentation tasks. We hope this challenging dataset would significantly contribute to the development of eye disease diagnosis and early prevention.

TLDR.value: We introduce the first video-based retinal vessel dataset (RVD), a collection of 635 smartphone-based videos with detailed vessel annotation.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
